beginner: Dill likes loose, well-drained soil and is not fussy about richness; it actually does fine in lean ground. Mix in a little compost so the soil holds some moisture but still drains freely. Heavy, soggy, or compacted soil is the main thing to avoid, since it rots the slow-sprouting seed and the deep little taproot. Steady moisture keeps the feathery leaves tender.
seasoned: Dill grows in most soils but does best in a loose, well-drained loam or sandy loam, and it tolerates poorer, leaner ground than most herbs. Utah State University describes it as a plant for well-drained, low-fertility to moderately fertile soil, so heavy feeding and very rich beds are unnecessary and can leave it lank. Work a little compost into the top few inches before sowing to hold even moisture, but do not overdo richness. It dislikes damp, poorly drained ground, which invites damping-off of the slow-germinating seed and leaf disease. Dill forms a slender taproot and resents transplanting, so it is best direct-sown into loosened soil.

beginner: Dill grows best in slightly acidic soil, about 5.5 to 6.5. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.5, slightly acidic; Utah State University gives this as dill's ideal range. It is forgiving and still does fine up to neutral, roughly 5.5 to 7.0. Dill is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Dill does not need much fertilizer and even grows well in poor soil. Mix a little compost into the bed before planting, and that is usually all it needs. If the soil is poor, you can give one light feeding while the plants are young. Too much fertilizer makes dill floppy and weakens the flavor, so go easy.
seasoned: Dill is a light feeder and one of the few herbs that prefers lean soil; Utah State University notes that no additional nutrients are needed if the soil is amended at planting. Work a little compost in before sowing and, in poor ground, give one light feeding once the plants are growing. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes dill lank and floppy and can dull the aromatic oils that give the leaves and seed their flavor. A plant grown on for seed or pickling heads needs no extra feeding once it bolts.

beginner: Your dill can take one light feeding now if the soil is poor.
seasoned: If your dill is in poor soil, you can give it one light feeding now.

beginner: Dill needs very little feeding. Mix compost into the soil at planting, and only feed lightly if the soil is poor.
seasoned: Dill is a light feeder that prefers lean soil; compost worked in at planting usually covers it, with at most one light, balanced feeding in poor ground. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes the plant floppy and weakens the aromatic oils.

beginner: Usually just compost at planting. If you feed, use a light all-purpose fertilizer once, at the label rate.
seasoned: Compost worked in at planting is usually enough; in poor soil, one light side-dress of a balanced fertilizer at the label rate while the plants are young.

beginner: Plump green caterpillars banded with black and yellow-orange dots, chewing the feathery leaves. They can strip a young plant, but on an established dill they usually do only light damage.
seasoned: Larvae of the black swallowtail (Papilio polyxenes), banded green, black, and yellow, feed on the foliage. On an established dill the defoliation is usually light and cosmetic; a heavy load can strip a seedling.

beginner: These are the caterpillars of the black swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs on dill and other carrot-family plants. They are also a welcome garden visitor, since they turn into a beautiful butterfly.
seasoned: Dill is a larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly. The caterpillars are a feature as much as a pest, so dill is often planted deliberately to support them.

beginner: On a big plant, just leave them; the damage is minor and you get butterflies. If they threaten a small planting, pick them off by hand and move them to a spare dill plant.
seasoned: On established plants, tolerate them, the feeding is minor and the butterflies are a benefit; on small plantings, handpick and relocate to a sacrificial dill. Bt is effective if control is truly needed, but is rarely warranted on a host plant grown partly for the butterflies.

beginner: Grow a little extra dill so there is enough to share with the caterpillars, and simply relocate them rather than spraying.
seasoned: Manage by tolerance and a little surplus planting rather than control: grow enough dill to share, relocate larvae from plants you want to protect, and reserve sprays for genuine seedling threats.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of the feathery leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
seasoned: Colonies of aphids gather on growing tips and leaf undersides; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop used fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Dill's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on dill; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. Dill itself, allowed to flower, is a strong insectary that recruits aphid predators.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Dill's own flowers also draw in ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which dill's own umbel flowers attract.

beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; letting some dill flower draws in the aphid predators it is famous for hosting.

beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves and flower stalks, usually later in the crop and in warm, dry-day weather. Heavily coated leaves yellow and are unpleasant to eat.
seasoned: A white, talc-like fungal growth on the foliage and stems, the most commonly noted fungal disease of dill, that builds in warm days with cool humid nights, in crowded stands, and where plants are overwatered; coated leaves lose quality.

beginner: A fungal disease that coats the leaves in white powder, favored by warm days, cool nights, crowding, and overwatering.
seasoned: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe heraclei on Apiaceae), favored by warm days, cool humid nights, dense stands with poor airflow, and excess moisture. Utah State University notes dill mildews when overwatered.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the planting for airflow, and avoid crowding and overhead watering. Most home crops are picked before it does much harm.
seasoned: Improve airflow with wider spacing, remove affected leaves, avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering; the leaf crop is usually cut before mildew matters, but a tall plant held for seed is more exposed.

beginner: Space plants for airflow, avoid crowding and overfeeding, and water at the base rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, avoid heavy nitrogen and overwatering, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for seed.

beginner: Small tan to brown spots, sometimes with a yellow halo, that spread on the leaves and can merge until the leaflets wilt and die back, worst in wet weather.
seasoned: Small tan-brown leaf lesions, sometimes yellow-haloed, that expand and coalesce until leaflets blight and die; favored by wet, splashy conditions and prolonged leaf wetness. Cercospora leaf blight (Cercosporidium punctum) and Alternaria leaf spot are the documented agents on dill.

beginner: Fungal leaf diseases that spread on wet leaves and splashing water and can arrive on infected seed. Spotted, blighted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Foliar fungi, chiefly Cercosporidium punctum (Cercospora blight) and Alternaria spp., spread by splash, wind, and infected seed and favored by warm, wet weather and overhead irrigation.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. There is no spray cure in the home garden, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, avoid overhead irrigation, space for airflow, rotate away from the carrot family, and remove infected debris; there is no effective home-garden cure once it is established.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, rotate the bed, and clear infected debris.
seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the fungi over.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where dill's slow germination leaves seed sitting in the danger zone.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting dill seed sits a long time before emerging.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows dill's already slow germination favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up faster.
seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh, viable seed.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week, especially while the plants are young.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept reasonably even; dill is fairly drought-tolerant once established but bolts faster and grows lank under heat and dry stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm and dry.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in warm, dry spells; once established dill takes some drought, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and slows the bolt.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks powdery mildew and leaf spot on a crop used fresh.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mildewed or mushy in soggy soil.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and powdery mildew or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than you want.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and faster bolting; drought stress hurries the plant toward its flower stalk and seed.

beginner: Dill is slow to sprout, so keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up.
seasoned: Dill germinates slowly, so keep the seedbed evenly moist through emergence, especially while the seedlings are young.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture through the first weeks of leaf growth.

beginner: Established dill takes some drought, but even water, about an inch a week, keeps the leaves tender and slows bolting. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry.
seasoned: Dill is fairly drought-tolerant once established, but it bolts faster and grows lank under heat and dry stress, so keep a reasonably even inch a week. Even moisture keeps the leaves tender and slows the bolt; water at the soil line to keep the lacy foliage dry against powdery mildew and leaf spot.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you cut the leaves. A hot, dry spell makes dill bolt sooner and turn coarse.
seasoned: Keep reasonably even moisture through the leaf-cutting weeks; a hot, dry check pushes the plant to flower and set seed sooner and coarsens the foliage.

beginner: As dill flowers and makes seed heads, ease off the water. If you want dill seed, a dry finish helps the heads ripen on the plant.
seasoned: As dill sends up its flower heads and sets seed, the leaf crop winds down; ease off watering, and for dill seed a drier finish helps the heads ripen and dry on the plant.

beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender and the plant does not bolt as early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps dill growing tender and slows the bolt; hot, dry spells push it to flower and set seed sooner and coarsen the foliage.

seasoned: Steady moisture through germination, which is slow in dill, and through the first weeks of leaf growth matters most; an established plant tolerates more drought.

beginner: Plant dill straight in the garden from seed, because it has a deep little root and does not like being moved. Sow the seeds about a quarter inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since young plants handle light frost. The seeds are slow, often taking two to three weeks, so keep the soil moist. Thin the plants to about 8 to 12 inches apart, and sow again every couple of weeks for a steady supply. In hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat makes it bolt; a summer crop is really for the seed and pickling heads.
seasoned: Dill is almost always direct-sown, since it forms a slender taproot and resents transplanting. Sow seed about 0.25 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; young dill tolerates light frost, so Wisconsin Horticulture suggests sowing a week or two before the last hard frost, and it germinates slowly, often 10 to 21 days. Sow a little thicker than the final stand and thin to 8 to 12 inches for full plants, or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady leaf supply. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since summer heat and long days bolt the crop to seed; midsummer plantings are grown for seed and pickling heads rather than leaves.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix, deep enough for dill's taproot.

beginner: Mix in a little compost for steady moisture; dill does not need rich soil.
seasoned: Blend in a little compost; dill is a light feeder, so avoid heavy fertilizer that leaves it lank in a pot.

seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress bolts dill.

beginner: Feed only lightly, since dill prefers lean soil and too much fertilizer makes potted dill floppy.
seasoned: Container dill needs only a light feed, if any; it prefers lean soil and overfeeding in a pot makes it floppy and weakens the flavor.

beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown dill can keep growing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot, since young dill takes light frost. In cold areas dill is not very cold-hardy, so a hard freeze will kill it; bring a small pot indoors to a bright window or simply let a plant drop seed, since dill reseeds itself readily.
seasoned: Dill tolerates light frost when young, so a fall-sown container can carry a leaf crop through winter in mild zones. It is less cold-hardy than the hardiest greens, and a hard freeze kills it, so in cold zones move a small pot to a bright indoor window or an unheated but protected spot, or simply rely on its heavy self-seeding to return plants in spring rather than overwintering the parent.

beginner: Dwarf dill makes an easy container herb. Use a pot at least 10 inches deep to fit its root, choose a compact variety like Fernleaf so it does not get too tall and tippy, and snip the feathery leaves as you need them. Keep it watered, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in hot weather to slow bolting.
seasoned: Dill grows well in a container at least 10 inches deep to fit its taproot. Standard dill reaches 3 to 5 feet and gets top-heavy, so choose a dwarf, slow-bolting variety such as Fernleaf for pots. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast and drought triggers bolting, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in warm spells. A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns.

seasoned: A self-watering container suits dill well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and slow to bolt.

beginner: Dill has a deeper root than most herbs and grows tall, so use a pot at least 10 inches deep and pick a short, compact variety so it does not tip over.
seasoned: Dill has a slender taproot and grows tall, so give it depth and stability: a container at least 10 inches deep suits it, and a dwarf variety stays short enough not to topple. Width adds sowing area for cut leaf.

beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, cilantro, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley, cilantro, fennel, celery, parsnip, and dill itself. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (leaf blights, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.

beginner: Try not to grow dill or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, cilantro, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant dill after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Dill self-sows a lot, so pull up stray seedlings that pop up where you do not want them.
seasoned: Rotate dill and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share foliar blights, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow dill with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because dill self-sows heavily from bolted plants, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place if you are managing the family carefully.

beginner: Dill flowers (bolts) when it gets hot and the days are long, sending up a tall stalk, and leaf growth slows. To keep the leaves coming, grow it in the cool parts of the year, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, give afternoon shade when it is hot, and try slow-bolting or dwarf types like Fernleaf or Dukat. When it does bolt, do not fight it: let the plant flower and make seed heads for pickling and dried dill seed.
seasoned: Dill bolts once summer heat and long days set in, sending up a tall flower stalk, and the leafy growth narrows and slows as the plant shifts to seed and pickling heads. Keep the leaf window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop steadily, lean on a late-summer sowing for a fall leaf crop, choose slow-bolting or dwarf types (Fernleaf, Dukat, Hera) where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced. There is no real fix once it bolts, so the productive answer in heat is to stop fighting it and grow the plant on for seed heads and dried dill seed.

beginner: Dill bolts (sends up a tall flower stalk) when it gets hot and the days are long. It is not a mistake: the very same flowering gives you the seed heads for pickling and the dried dill seed used as a spice. The flowers are great for bees and helpful insects, and the plant often drops seed and comes up again on its own the next year. Grow it in cool weather for leaves, and let it bloom in summer for seed.
seasoned: Bolting in dill is driven by summer heat above roughly 75 to 80°F and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding. This is the defining rhythm of the crop: the same bolt that slows the leafy dill weed produces the flower heads and seed used for pickling and as the spice, so the plant is not failing, it is changing product. The yellow umbel flowers feed pollinators and beneficial insects strongly, and unharvested plants self-sow readily, often returning as volunteers the next spring. In hot regions the leaf window is short and growers deliberately let summer plantings run to seed and heads.

beginner: Do not leave cut dill out on the counter, where it wilts fast; either chill it or stand the stems in a glass of water. Dried dill seed keeps for months at room temperature.
seasoned: Fresh dill leaves wilt within a day or two at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days. Dried dill seed, by contrast, is shelf-stable for months once dried.

beginner: Store fresh dill unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps about a week. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate fresh dill leaves unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or stems standing in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; dill holds about a week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Dill freezes well for cooking. Chop it into an ice-cube tray with a little water or oil and freeze. For dill seed, let the seed heads dry on the plant, then store the seeds in a jar.
seasoned: Dill freezes well for cooking: chop the fronds into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or freeze them flat in bags, where the flavor holds better than dried. Dill seed is dried, not frozen: cut the seed heads as they turn tan, dry them, then thresh and store the seed airtight.

beginner: Use fresh dill within a week or so of picking, or freeze it. Dill seed is the opposite: dry the tan seed heads, shake out the seeds, and store them in a sealed jar for many months. Green seed heads are picked fresh for pickling.
seasoned: Fresh dill weed is delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week, or freeze it for cooking. The seed and heads are the keepers: harvest seed heads as they turn from green to tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, and the threshed dill seed stores airtight for months. Green seed heads are used fresh for pickling.

beginner: If you want leafy dill weed, pick a slow-bolting or dwarf variety like Fernleaf, Dukat, Hera, or Bouquet, which take a bit longer to flower. None of them stop flowering in heat, so sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks too. If you mainly want seed heads for pickling, grow a tall type like Long Island Mammoth.
seasoned: Match the type to the goal. For leafy dill weed, choose slow-bolting selections, Fernleaf (dwarf, for pots), Dukat, Hera, and Bouquet, which hold in leaf longer before the seedstalk rises; none truly stop the bolt in heat and long days, but they buy time. For seed and pickling heads, the tall heirlooms Long Island Mammoth and Mammoth set big heads fast and are the classic pickling dills. Because the bolt is inevitable in warmth, succession sowing matters as much as variety for a steady leaf supply.

beginner: Dill is one of the great companion herbs, mostly because of what it does when it flowers: the yellow blooms pull in hoverflies, ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids and caterpillars on nearby crops. It is a traditional partner for the cabbage family, where it is said to help against cabbageworms, and it interplants well with cucumbers, onions, lettuce, and corn. Keep it away from fennel, which can cross-pollinate it, and from carrots, its close relative.
seasoned: Most of dill's companion value is real but indirect: allowed to flower, dill (an Apiaceae umbel) is a strong insectary plant, recruiting hoverflies, ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids and caterpillars on neighboring crops, an effect extension IPM guidance leans on. It is a traditional companion for brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, kale), where folklore credits it with deterring cabbageworms, plausible via the beneficials it draws but not measured as a direct effect; it also interplants with cucumbers, onions, lettuce, and corn. The well-grounded cautions are its own carrot-family relatives: fennel and carrots, which can cross-pollinate dill where they flower together, and which share Apiaceae pests on rotation grounds.

beginner: Dill is a classic partner for the cabbage family. Let some dill flower nearby and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and cabbageworm caterpillars, and gardeners have long planted the two together.
seasoned: A traditional brassica pairing with a real mechanism: dill left to flower recruits hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids and caterpillars, including cabbageworms, on cole crops. Sound by the insectary mechanism and long tradition, not a measured dill-on-cabbage effect.

beginner: Dill and cucumbers are a kitchen and garden match, since you pickle cucumbers with dill, and they grow in an overlapping season; the flowering dill also draws in insects that help the cucumbers.
seasoned: A traditional culinary-and-garden pairing: cucumbers and dill share the pickling jar and an overlapping season, and flowering dill recruits beneficials that help cucumbers. Tradition plus the insectary mechanism, not a measured pair effect.

beginner: These grow alongside dill without crowding it, and the helpful insects dill's flowers attract spill over onto them. A simple, easygoing interplant.
seasoned: Complementary-habit interplants: onions, lettuce, and corn share space and season with dill without strong competition, and benefit from the beneficials its flowers draw. Structural and traditional, not a tested effect.

beginner: Keep dill away from carrots. They are close relatives, so if both flower they can cross-pollinate, and they share carrot-family pests and diseases.
seasoned: Dill and carrots are both Apiaceae and can cross-pollinate where both are allowed to flower for seed, and they share carrot-family pests and diseases on rotation grounds. The classic folklore that mature dill suppresses carrot growth is largely untested; keep them apart mainly for the cross-pollination and shared-pest reasons.

beginner: Keep dill away from fennel. They are carrot-family cousins that can cross-pollinate if both flower, muddling the flavor of saved seed, and fennel is a poor neighbor for many plants.
seasoned: Fennel is a fellow Apiaceae that can cross-pollinate dill where both bloom for seed, and it is a broad allelopath and classic poor herb neighbor that suppresses many plants. Give fennel its own corner. A traditional rule with a real mechanism, not a measured dill-fennel trial.

beginner: The first thin, grassy little leaves poking up. Dill is slow, often taking two to three weeks, so be patient and keep the soil moist.
seasoned: The first pair of narrow, thread-like seed leaves pushing up. Dill is slow to germinate, often 10 to 21 days, and emergence can be uneven, so be patient.

beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings are up, which can take a couple of weeks. Sow shallowly in cool weather.
seasoned: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but never waterlogged through the long germination window. Sow shallowly into cool soil, about 60 to 70°F; cold, soggy soil rots the slow seed.

beginner: Any sprouts yet?
seasoned: Any sprouts yet?

beginner: The first true feathery leaves. Now you can thin the seedlings.
seasoned: The first true leaves, finely divided and feathery. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.

beginner: Thin the seedlings to about 8 to 12 inches apart, and use the ones you pull. Keep the water steady.
seasoned: Thin to 8 to 12 inches for full plants, or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf, and use the thinnings in the kitchen. Keep moisture steady to delay the bolt.

beginner: How are they coming along?
seasoned: How are they coming along?

beginner: Bushy, feathery plants several inches tall, before any flower stalk appears.
seasoned: Bushy, feathery plants 8 to 12 inches tall, well before any central stalk rises. This is the productive dill-weed window.

beginner: Start picking the feathery leaves now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming. Keep the water steady so it does not bolt, and pick faster when it warms up.
seasoned: Start cutting feathery fronds now rather than waiting; regular cutting keeps tender new growth coming. Keep moisture even to hold off the bolt, and crop faster as the weather warms.

beginner: Ready to start cutting?
seasoned: Ready to start cutting?

beginner: Full, feathery leaves and no flower stalk in the middle yet. Once a tall stalk appears the leafy stage is ending.
seasoned: Full, tender feathery foliage with no central flower stalk yet. Once a thick stalk rises the leaf window narrows and the plant turns to flowering.

beginner: Snip the feathery leaves from the outside. Pick young in the cool morning, and once you see a flower stalk, either pick the last leaves or let it go to seed heads for pickling.
seasoned: Cut whole fronds from the outside or shear the upper plant for fresh dill weed. Pick young and in the cool morning, and as a plant shows a stalk, decide whether to keep it for seed heads.

beginner: Harvesting regularly?
seasoned: Harvesting regularly?

beginner: A tall stalk from the middle, then flat yellow flowers and green seeds. This is dill turning to seed heads, which you use for pickling.
seasoned: A tall central stalk shooting up, the foliage thinning, then flat yellow umbel flowers and green seed. This is the shift from leafy dill weed to flower heads and dill seed.

beginner: If you want leaves, pick everything good now. For pickling, cut the flower heads as they open; for dill seed, let the heads turn tan, then cut and dry them. Leave a plant alone and it often reseeds itself.
seasoned: For leaves, cut everything worth using before quality fades. For pickling heads, cut the umbels as the flowers open; for dried seed, let the heads turn tan but cut before they shatter, then dry them. Leave one plant to self-sow if you want volunteers.

seasoned: Seen a flower stalk yet?

beginner: Your dill seedlings should be big enough to thin. Space them out and use the little ones you pull.
seasoned: Your dill should have a true leaf or two now. Thin to 8 to 12 inches for full plants or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf, and use the thinnings.

beginner: Dill gives you two things from one plant: the soft feathery leaves are dill weed, and the flower heads and seeds are what you use for pickling and as a spice. Like cilantro, and unlike warm-season herbs such as basil, dill is a cool-leaning plant. Young plants handle a light frost, but once summer heat and long days arrive it bolts, sending up a tall flower stalk that can reach 3 to 5 feet, and leaf growth slows. So the trick is to grow it for leaves in the cooler parts of the year, spring and again in late summer for fall, and to let the summer plants flower for seed heads. Sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks, since each plant bolts after a while, and plant the seeds right in the garden because dill does not like being moved. It is fast, easy, and reseeds itself, so once you grow it you often get volunteers the next year. And when it bolts, you get dill heads for pickling and dried dill seed.
seasoned: Dill (Anethum graveolens) is an annual herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae) grown for two products from one plant: the feathery leaves are the herb dill weed, and the flower heads and dried seed are used for pickling and as the spice dill seed. Like cilantro, and unlike warm-season herbs such as basil, dill is a cool-leaning crop that bolts once summer heat and long days arrive, sending up a tall flower stalk (the plant reaches 3 to 5 feet in flower) above roughly 75 to 80°F. That shapes how it is grown: the leaf crop favors the cool shoulders of the year, spring and especially a late-summer-into-fall sowing, while the heat of summer is when growers let it run to seed and pickling heads rather than leaves. Because the bolt is fast and inevitable in warmth, dill is a succession crop, sown in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks so fresh, pre-bolt plants keep coming. It is direct-sown (a slender taproot resents transplanting), young plants tolerate light frost, and it self-sows so readily that a patch often returns on its own. It is easy and largely trouble-free, with the black swallowtail caterpillar a welcome visitor as much as a pest. The grower's real skill is timing the leaf crop into the cool seasons and treating the summer bolt as the start of the seed-and-pickling harvest rather than a failure.

beginner: Start picking dill when the plants are 8 to 10 inches tall and bushy, a few weeks after sowing and before you see a tall flower stalk. Snip the feathery leaves from the outside, and pick in the cool morning for the best flavor. Pick often, because once it bolts the plant puts its energy into flowers and seed. For pickling, cut the flower heads as the blooms open. For dried dill seed, let the heads turn tan, cut and dry them, then shake out the seeds to store.
seasoned: Begin cutting dill leaves once plants are 8 to 10 inches tall and bushy, roughly 6 to 8 weeks from sowing, well before the central seedstalk rises. Snip whole feathery fronds from the outside, or shear the upper plant, taking no more than a third at a time and picking in the cool morning for the best flavor; pick often, since the leaf window closes once it bolts. For green pickling heads, cut the umbels just as the flowers open and the immature seed forms. For dried dill seed, let the plant flower and set seed and harvest the heads as they turn from green to tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, then thresh and store the seed airtight.
